definition.text: A sequential game in which a leader firm chooses its quantity first and follower firms then respond, competing on quantity.

facts.text: Heinrich von Stackelberg described it in 1934; it needs a leader with commitment power, and the follower must observe the leader's move and be unable to commit to other actions.
It is solved by backward induction: the leader anticipates the follower's best response and picks the quantity maximising its own payoff.
Moving first gives the leader an advantage over Cournot; if the follower cannot observe the leader's move, the game reduces to Cournot.
Stackelberg output exceeds Cournot output but is below Bertrand output, and its price is lower than Cournot's but higher than Bertrand's.
Stackelberg price lies below the monopoly or cartel price but above the perfectly competitive price.

title: Vertical integration

definition.text: An arrangement in which a company owns and controls several stages of its supply chain.

facts.text: It contrasts with horizontal integration, where a company produces several related items; it comes as backward (upstream), forward (downstream) or balanced.
A firm integrates to secure the supplies it needs and the market for its product, but it becomes undesirable when it turns anti-competitive.
The real net output ratio, added value over total production value, measures it; the less a firm outsources, the closer the ratio is to one.

Gains include synchronising supply and demand, capturing upstream or downstream margins and lower uncertainty; losses include higher switching costs, weaker performance incentives upstream and specific investments.
For society, it can lower consumer prices by cutting intermediary markups, but it can enable price manipulation where market power is established.
In the US, 90% of poultry, 69% of hogs and 29% of cattle are produced under contracts that act as vertical integration.

Before late-20th-century deregulation, most US electric utilities were vertically integrated across generation, transmission, distribution and sales; PURPA in 1978 forced them to buy outside power if competitive, giving rise to independent producers.

related: Transaction cost theory of the firm
